summary:
Orbit Keepers is an educational browser game created by Los Galaktikos, a team of four students from TED Eskişehir College in Türkiye. Players pilot a recovery spacecraft, collect space debris and protect working satellites while managing a limited oxygen supply.

Across three two-minute stages, players face faster oxygen loss and more hazards. They earn credits to upgrade their equipment and decide which routes are worth the risk. Turkish satellites, including Türksat, Göktürk and İMECE, appear as protected spacecraft that cannot be collected.

The project addresses Space Mission Design Game through resource management, equipment choices and mission outcomes. NASA educational resources and Earth imagery support the game, while NASA mission-design guidance informs our project analysis. Our goal is to help young players understand space debris and learn how careful decisions can protect useful spacecraft and keep a mission alive.
details:
Our project

Orbit Keepers is an educational browser game developed by Los Galaktikos, a team of four students from TED Eskişehir College in Türkiye. Players pilot a small recovery spacecraft, collect space debris and protect working satellites while managing oxygen. We want young players to understand that a successful mission requires careful decisions, not just a high score.

How it works

Players steer with WASD, arrow keys or hold-and-drag controls. A fictional tractor field attracts nearby recoverable debris. Retired satellites award 30 points, used rocket stages 20 and panel fragments 10. Each recovery sends a TED credit logo towards the score display.

The game has three stages, each lasting two minutes. Oxygen decreases by five points every three seconds in stage one, five points every two seconds in stage two and ten points every second in stage three. Every ten recoveries restores five oxygen points. Red fragments cause ten points of oxygen loss on impact and become more frequent in later stages. At low oxygen, a red warning and an audible alarm alert the player when sound effects are enabled. Reaching zero oxygen ends the run.

Between successful stages, players can buy at most one suit upgrade. Tank capacity increases from 100 to 125 and then 150, while upgraded equipment extends the tractor range. The next stage starts with a full tank. Players must balance collection opportunities, dangerous clusters and equipment choices.

Protecting working satellites

Our game represents Türksat 3A, 4A, 4B, 5A, 5B and 6A, Göktürk-1, Göktürk-2 and İMECE as protected spacecraft. One appears at a time for seven seconds, with clear space around it. These satellites cannot be collected.

We included them to introduce Türkiye’s communications and observation spacecraft and show that useful satellites must be protected. They are illustrative models, not satellite photographs, live telemetry or accurate orbital simulations. The TED Eskişehir College emblem connects the project to our school.

Connection to Space Mission Design Game

Orbit Keepers explores the operational side of the challenge through limited resources, equipment decisions, increasing risk and mission results. A dense debris cluster offers more collection opportunities but may contain dangerous fragments.

Our prototype is a focused recovery scenario. It does not yet include launch selection, scientific payload design, mass and power budgets, real orbital calculations or cooperative multiplayer. These are possible future developments.

NASA resources and scientific accuracy

NASA’s educational article about orbital debris supports the debris categories and collision-safety background. NASA Blue Marble imagery provides Earth context. During documentation review, we also applied the challenge-listed NASA resource Design and Develop Science Missions to analyse our mission scope and concept of operations. The project report explains these uses and provides source links.

The game does not use a live NASA API or a NASA trajectory engine. Debris does not produce breathable oxygen: the recovery bonus is a fictional game reward. The tractor field, accelerated oxygen consumption and planetary arrangement are also simplified mechanics.

Technology

The project uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Canvas 2D. It runs in a browser and is hosted on Niobe. Firebase Anonymous Authentication and Cloud Firestore support shared flight records, completed-run archives and an approximate browser visitor count. Local scores provide a fallback when shared services are unavailable.

Country flags use approximate IP-based country estimates from country.is. VPNs and network routing can affect the result. Our Firestore records store a country code rather than the raw IP address.

Team contributions and development support

A.B.Y. contributed the game concept, rules and design. B.I. contributed visual decisions. M.K.Ç. researched NASA resources and Turkish satellites. D.K. tested the game. Our mentor is Zümrüt ÖZMEN, Physics Teacher.

Adult coordination and substantial OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT assistance supported code generation and revision, debugging, visual implementation, automated checks and English documentation. We do not present the implementation as unaided student coding.

The soundtrack was generated with Suno by Ahmet Engin YILMAZ and supplied with permission for Orbit Keepers, its demo and presentation.

Testing and intended impact

An assisted live test completed all three stages through normal controls, reaching 95,080 points with 100 of 150 oxygen points remaining. The game confirmed that the completed result was archived online. This software check is separate from the student testing contribution and is not evidence of a measured classroom learning outcome.

We hope the game encourages players to discuss space debris, recognise working satellites and explain how limited resources affect their decisions. Future improvements could include mission planning, more realistic equipment trade-offs, accessibility improvements and teacher-led learning evaluation.
